newsitem.title: USA: Nuveen conf analyst says structure key, not rating.
newsitem.headline: Nuveen conf analyst says structure key, not rating.

text.p: It's the structure of a deal, not necessarily a bond rating, that makes a housing issue attractive to investors, an analyst attending the John Nuveen & Co Inc annual state housing conference here this week said.

Issuers also should find a definite market for uninsured bonds in the multi-family finance arena, while investors considering elder care facilities should be cautioned about the possibility of future overbuilding in the unregulated industry, analysts said.
Eaton Vance Management housing analyst Nick Combs told issuers that state housing authorities need not concern themselves with obtaining a rating in most instances.

"From my perspective, it almost doesn't matter," Combs said. "Most housing finance authorities are well-managed and have good credit and there's not much of a difference, that's not to say I wouldn't look at it."
Nuveen housing researcher Justin Craib Cox and Illinois Housing Executive Director John Varones said they see some value in obtaining ratings.
A rating could be more helpful on the multi-family housing side, but there is a lot of volume on the single family side, Combs said.
On the single-family side, investors need consistent offerings, a clear structure, more and more timely disclosure and specifics on the projects being financed, Combs said.
Updating state housing agency disclosures on Internet sites would benefit investors significantly as well, analysts said.
Uninsured bonds hold value for investors and issuers faced with the rapid growth of insured offerings, Janet D'Ambrosio said.

Most finance housing authority bonds are strong enough without insurance, said D'Ambrosio, research analyst for Massachusetts Financial Services. Portfolio managers faced with requirements for holding a certain percentage of insured and uninsured debt could also raise the demand for uninsured bonds, she said.
Insurance can also mask pitfalls in call features for an unwary investor as well, D'Ambrosio added.

While there is tremendous growth in the elder care field, investors should be cautious and aware of the likelihood of radical changes affecting facilities over the possible 30-year life of a bond, said Karen Szerszen, a research analyst for Allstate Insurance Cos.

With no required certificate of need process, as regulates the hospital field, there is a real potential for overbuilding, Szerszen said. Investors should follow the facilities management and note that the taste's of prospective residents will change over time, she said.

Investors must see at least 10 percent equity from developers to make the projects attractive, Szerszen said. Expansions of existing well-managed facilities are more attractive as are those which operate on rental basis, rather than requiring an endowment from residents, she said.
